title: {{NAME}} and the League of Impossible Defenders
moral: The team that learns from losing honestly will, in time, beat the team that has only ever known how to win.

pages.content:
The Ironclad Stadium rose from the industrial quarter of Port Voss like something that had grown there rather than been built, its walls riveted steel, its floodlights shaped like enormous mechanical fists holding searchlights aloft. It was the home of the Iron Defenders, the most consistently undefeated football team in the city's long and competitive history.

They had not lost a match in seven years.

The Iron Defenders were two things at once: three human players, each of whom happened to be a superhero, and five robots, each custom-built for a specific role, and the combination had proved, over seven unbeaten years, to be effectively unstoppable.

{{NAME}} arrived at the stadium in the first grey light of morning, the day before the championship match, because he had been asked to. The invitation had come from an unusual source: UNIT 7, the team's central midfielder, who had sent it by electronic message at two in the morning with a subject line that read PROBLEM.

UNIT 7 was waiting inside the main entrance, a compact and precise robot with sensor-eyes the colour of fresh copper, its posture the careful, balanced stillness of something that has been engineered for efficiency and has also, beyond the engineering, developed opinions.

'You came early,' UNIT 7 said.

'You sent the message at two in the morning,' {{NAME}} said.

'Yes,' said UNIT 7. 'I was concerned. I could not sleep. I do not sleep. But if I did, I would have been unable to.'

pages.content:
The problem was this: one of the human players, a superhero named Dex who played left wing and possessed the specific gift of accelerating faster than physics generally allowed, had injured himself in training.

He would play anyway. Everyone knew Dex would play anyway. The problem was not his injury.

The problem was that for the first time in seven years, the Iron Defenders were genuinely uncertain. And none of them knew how to play while uncertain, because they had never had to.

{{NAME}} watched the morning session from the technical area. UNIT 7 was flawless, as always, distributing the ball with metronomic precision to positions calculated three moves ahead. The two remaining human players, a superhero striker named Jace and a goalkeeper named Brin who could read the trajectory of any shot before it was struck, performed with their habitual brilliance.

But there was a rigidity to it. An over-careful quality. They were playing not to win but not to lose, and there is an enormous and specific difference.

Dex sat in the stands watching with his knee wrapped and his face carefully neutral, and UNIT 7 kept glancing toward the stands at intervals too regular to be accidental.

'It is checking on him,' {{NAME}} said to no one in particular.

UNIT 7 heard him from thirty metres away. 'He is the variable I cannot calculate,' UNIT 7 said, without breaking stride. 'I know every player's movement profile. I do not know what he will do when he is afraid.'

pages.content:
The match went wrong in the thirty-first minute.

Dex was playing, of course, because Dex always played. He had accelerated twice on the left in the first half and both times it had gone well enough, though {{NAME}} could see the slight alteration in how he placed the injured leg, the fraction of hesitation that anyone watching carefully could read.

The opposition could read it too. They targeted the left flank. Not cruelly, but cleverly, as good opponents do.

When Dex was dispossessed for the second time, the goal came quickly. 1-0 down, first time the Defenders had conceded at home in three seasons.

The stadium went completely silent.

UNIT 7 collected the ball from the net with the precise, unhurried movement of a machine that does not panic, and walked it back to the centre circle. On the way, it stopped beside Dex.

Everyone expected some kind of tactical communication. UNIT 7 was the tactical heart of the team. It would recalibrate, redistribute, account for the variable.

UNIT 7 said: 'You were the best left winger I have ever calculated. The data says so. Not as you were last month. As you are today, here, now, injured and still here.'

Dex stared at the robot for a moment that stretched longer than the match permitted.

Then Dex laughed, short and surprised, the way you laugh when something lands in the one place you forgot to guard.

'Get the ball,' Dex said. 'Come on.'

pages.content:
The second half was something different from anything the Ironclad Stadium had seen in seven unbeaten years, which was precisely because it was not unbeaten.

The Iron Defenders were playing from behind. They were uncertain and careful and fractionally wrong-footed, and they were playing anyway, all of them, with a quality that the crowd had never had occasion to see from this team because it could only appear when everything else was stripped away.

Jace created an equaliser from nothing, turning twice in a tight space and finding a gap that Brin, at the other end of the pitch, had predicted by some goalkeeper's alchemy and pointed at before Jace had even turned. UNIT 7 built everything from the centre with a consistency that was no longer just mechanical. Something else had entered its play, something that processed variables beyond trajectory and distribution.

Dex, on his injured leg, made one run. A single run, in the seventy-eighth minute, perfectly timed, the injured leg planted once and held. The cross he produced from it was curling and exact.

Jace met it at the far post.

2-1.

{{NAME}} was on his feet in the technical area without having decided to stand. The crowd, enormous and overwhelming, were all on their feet. The sound was not the roar of a team that had won again. It was the sound of a crowd that had seen something. It was different. Everyone in the stadium could feel the difference.

Brin caught the last shot of the match with the serene certainty of someone who had already decided, long before the ball was struck, that it would not go in.

pages.content:
The trophy room already had seven championship shields on its wall, and they hung a new one alongside them that night, identical in shape but somehow distinct in quality, the way one year of a life can contain more than seven others combined.

Dex stood in front of it for a long time.

UNIT 7 stood beside him, and {{NAME}} stood beside UNIT 7, and none of them said anything for a while, which was its own kind of conversation.

'Will you come back?' UNIT 7 asked eventually. 'For next season.'

{{NAME}} thought about it. He was not a superhero. He could not accelerate beyond physics or read shot trajectories or calculate three moves ahead. He was good at watching, and good at being present, and apparently good at being asked to help by robots who sent messages at two in the morning.

'Yes,' he said.

UNIT 7's copper eyes brightened by a fraction that a person might not have noticed, though {{NAME}} had been looking for it.

He walked home through Port Voss, the stadium lights still blazing behind him, the streets of the industrial quarter warm with the after-sound of the crowd.

He fell asleep quickly, the particular satisfied weight of a good difficult day in every part of him.

And in the morning, there was already another message from UNIT 7, time-stamped three fourteen in the morning, subject line: IDEA FOR NEXT SEASON. SEE WHAT YOU THINK.
